title: Knowledge Check 8: Lessons 57-64
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 57-64 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Within a serverless platform, what is the main design consequence of the hard cap on how long one invocation may run?
options: It changes nothing, because a warmed execution environment can be reused across an effectively unlimited run of separate invocations that keep reusing the same warm container
It forces fast request-response work to fit inside the cap while durable batch work is consumed one unit per invocation behind a queue
It means a single invocation must run an agent's entire loop to completion before it may return any answer to the caller
It applies only to edge runtimes and never to container-based services such as a request-driven container platform
questions.explanation: Because each invocation has a fixed time budget, a long agent task cannot run in one call: fast answers return within the cap, while the batch backlog is drained one unit of work per invocation behind a queue.

questions.question: Which pair of signals does a request-driven container platform use to size its running instance count?
options: Queue depth and GPU utilization, so a background agent scales on the length of its pending backlog of jobs
Memory utilization alone, so an agent that is memory heavy is given fewer but larger instances to run on
Average CPU utilization and average request concurrency
A fixed replica count set once at deploy time, so the fleet size never changes as live traffic rises and falls
questions.explanation: Instance count is driven by average CPU utilization and average request concurrency, clamped between configured minimum and maximum limits, so an interactive agent scales with the number of callers it is serving at once.

questions.question: Why does streaming a model's output matter for agents hosted on a platform whose instances disappear after a request?
options: Because a short-lived instance can still send tokens as they are produced, so the reply feels live even though the instance is gone
Because streaming stores each conversation turn inside the instance so the state can be reused on a later request without an external store
Because streaming is a hard requirement of every edge runtime, and a function that does not stream is refused at deploy time on all platforms
Because streaming lets the function skip the model provider call entirely and answer straight from its cached parameters
questions.explanation: A stateless instance can vanish the moment its request ends, but streaming returns tokens and tool messages as they are produced, so the user experiences a continuous live reply rather than a long pause.

questions.question: What does quantizing a model do to its memory footprint?
options: It stores each weight in fewer bits, cutting the memory footprint roughly fourfold at 4-bit versus 16-bit
It rewrites the model's architecture so that fewer parameters are needed to represent the same task at run time
It changes only the model's training cost and leaves the memory the model needs at run time completely unchanged
It compresses the tokenizer vocabulary alone, while the weight tensors still load into memory at full precision
questions.explanation: Quantization stores each parameter in fewer bits, so a full-precision model that would not fit drops to roughly a quarter of its size at 4-bit, at the cost of some quality.

questions.question: Using the standard rule of thumb, about how much memory should an 11-billion-parameter model's weights need at 4-bit?
options: About 2 GB, because parameter count has little to do with memory
About 6.6 GB, budgeting roughly 0.6 GB per billion parameters
About 22 GB, because every parameter needs two bytes no matter how it is stored
Exactly 11 GB, because one billion parameters always equals one gigabyte
questions.explanation: The rule of thumb is roughly 0.6 GB of memory per billion parameters at 4-bit, so 11 billion parameters land near 6.6 GB before context-window and runtime headroom.

questions.question: For a single user on local hardware, what mainly caps how fast a model generates tokens?
options: How fast memory can move the model's weights into the compute units, roughly bandwidth divided by bytes of model
How many concurrent users are sharing the machine, which fixes a per-user speed regardless of what hardware is present
The network round trip between the machine and the model provider, since even a local build still needs a hosted API at run time
The exact spelling of the prompt text, because tokenization alone dominates every latency figure measured on the machine
questions.explanation: For one user, speed is bounded by how quickly weights stream from memory into the compute units, so a smaller quantized model moves fewer bytes per token and feels faster.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a router and a cascade?
options: A router makes one model choice up front, while a cascade starts cheap and escalates on a failed check
A router calls models one after another in turn, while a cascade makes a single choice before the call begins
A router is always a hand-written rule, while a cascade is always a classifier trained on preference data
A router lowers latency, while a cascade lowers cost, and each leaves the other measure untouched
questions.explanation: A router picks the model once before the call, while a cascade runs the cheap model first and escalates to a stronger one only when a consistency or confidence check fails.

questions.question: Why is sending every request to the frontier model usually the wrong default for an agent?
options: Frontier models are slower on every input, so a small model always wins on both quality and cost across the workload
Frontier models can only be called a fixed number of times per day, so most traffic must be spread across cheaper models
Most requests are simple enough for a small model, so a frontier price on all of them buys no better answer
Small models return the same outputs as frontier models on every input, so the choice of model never actually matters
questions.explanation: Easy requests such as classification or short extraction are handled well by a small model, so paying frontier per-token pricing on all of them spends premium compute where it does not change the answer.

questions.question: Even with good routing, which traffic should stay on the strong model by rule rather than by a difficulty score?
options: Short classification and extraction calls, because they are by far the cheapest of all the work to send to a small model instead
Security, financial, and adversarial input, because routing is a cost lever and not a security boundary
Any ticket the small model has already answered once, to avoid re-running the whole pipeline
High-difficulty tickets only, since a difficulty score settles every other case on its own
questions.explanation: Routing is a cost lever, not a security boundary, so privileged or adversarial traffic is held on the strong model by rule instead of being left to a difficulty score.

questions.question: Which of the three LLM caching layers can serve a wrong answer to a different question?
options: Provider prefix caching, because it reuses a repeated prompt prefix that the provider bills at a discount
Exact-match response caching, because it hashes the whole normalized request and expects a byte-identical match
Semantic caching, because it matches on embedding similarity by a threshold rather than on an exact match
None of the layers, because each one only ever returns a response that is identical to the request it stored
questions.explanation: Semantic caching matches by embedding similarity against a threshold, so embedding-close inputs can be treated as meaning-equal and a stored answer for one question can be served for another.

questions.question: What is the similarity threshold in a semantic cache best understood as?
options: A precision-and-recall knob: a low value raises the hit rate but risks answering a question that was not asked
A fixed constant that every route should share, because a single global value always fits every route just as well
A setting that only changes embedding cost and has no bearing on which stored answers are served to a caller
A cap on how many cached entries a route may keep before the oldest entries are evicted from the store
questions.explanation: The threshold trades precision against recall: lowering it raises the hit rate but lets looser matches through, while raising it makes the cache safe but closer to exact-match caching.

questions.question: Why should the system-prompt version be part of a semantic cache's namespace?
options: Because system prompts never change in practice, so the version tag is only ever useful for audit logging
Because encoding the version into the key measurably improves the embedding model's similarity scores
Because it is unnecessary, since a time-to-live alone always expires every stale entry long before any user is ever served one
Because bumping the version rolls the cache forward, so answers from an older prompt are never matched again
questions.explanation: The namespace encodes a version, and bumping it rolls the cache forward, so stale answers produced under an older prompt are never served after the prompt changes.

questions.question: A question asks who approved a budget and which direct reports of that person touched the record. Which memory backend fits, and why?
options: Vector memory, because it matches the query by meaning against past message chunks and stored conversation text on similarity
A knowledge graph, because the question follows explicit approval and reporting links that similarity cannot trace
A flat keyword index, because the question turns on exact string matches across the stored records and fields
Neither store, because this is a prompt-engineering problem with no memory backend involved at all
questions.explanation: The question follows an approval chain and a reporting chain, which are explicit relationships; a knowledge graph represents entities as nodes and those links as typed edges, so traversal answers what similarity cannot.

questions.question: A team needs an agent that recalls broad topics from prior sessions and tolerates paraphrased reminders. Following the recommended growth path, what should it build first?
options: A knowledge graph up front, so that exact relationships are captured from the very first session onward without any delay
A relational table of keyword tags indexed across every past conversation and every stored session for fast lookup
A vector store for fast fuzzy recall, adding a knowledge graph later for high-value entities
Only the context window, with no external memory store kept at all
questions.explanation: Vector memory is the fast, fuzzy default with low setup cost, so the growth path starts with a vector store for broad recall and adds a knowledge graph only when relational questions demand it.

questions.question: In the hybrid retrieval pattern, what job does the vector search do and what job does the graph traversal do?
options: The vectors resolve the relational path while the graph runs the fuzzy similarity search over stored text passages
The vectors find entry points and candidate entities, and traversal follows relationships outward
Both stores run the identical query on every turn and their results are averaged into one answer
The graph stores the embedding vectors while the vector store holds the typed edges between entities
questions.explanation: The hybrid uses vectors to find the entry points and candidate entities, then traverses the graph outward from those points to pull precise relational context.

questions.question: Why can vector similarity search fail on a question that aggregates over a whole collection, such as counting all open tickets?
options: Because it retrieves the most similar items and treats them as the whole population, not the entire collection
Because it always returns exactly four results and cannot be configured to return a larger number at all
Because a vector store holds edges rather than text, so any numeric aggregation over the data is impossible
Because it refuses to answer any question that does not contain an exact keyword match somewhere in the stored text of the collection
questions.explanation: Similarity search returns the nearest items and the model assumes those are the whole set, so it cannot reason about the shape of an entire collection the way an aggregation query over the graph can.

questions.question: In the standard graph retrieval loop, what step comes right after linking the query's entities to the matching nodes?
options: Extracting the entities, relationships, and metadata from the source data during the ingestion pass
Traversing the graph by generating a graph query that walks the relationships the question needs
Re-embedding the entire graph so the vector index reflects the new connections
Generating the response and layering the retrieved graph context into the prompt
questions.explanation: The loop runs extract, link, traverse, then generate, so after the query's entities are linked to nodes the next step is to traverse the relationships with a generated graph query.

questions.question: Which three question shapes does a knowledge graph genuinely beat plain vector memory on?
options: Text-similarity lookups, full-text keyword searches, and linguistic paraphrase recall across a document set
Standalone fact lookups, single-document summaries, and token-length optimization targets
Relationship-path multi-hop queries, whole-corpus aggregations, and dense interconnected domains
Image retrieval, numeric range filters, and fuzzy date matching across log files
questions.explanation: A graph wins where resemblance fails: relationship-path multi-hop questions, whole-corpus aggregations, and dense interconnected domains where everything looks similar to everything else.

questions.question: Why treat prompts with the same version-tracking as code?
options: Because it shortens the file name and makes each prompt easier to type into a terminal during a deployment
Because two prompts can be a comma apart yet behave completely differently, so history and rollback matter
Because it is the only format an open-source evaluation tool will accept when it runs the test cases
Because it forces a full application redeploy on every wording change, which is the intended safety net
questions.explanation: Prompts are production behavior: two nearly identical prompts can behave very differently, so a real version history, a rollback path, and a record of which version runs where are all needed.

questions.question: Why does a regression suite matter more for a prompt than for an ordinary function?
options: Because a renamed function breaks the build at once, while a reworded prompt breaks nothing until users hit it
Because a prompt has a compiler that catches every wording mistake in the editor before the change is saved
Because a regression suite rewrites the prompt into a syntax that the model parses measurably faster at run time
Because the suite signs the prompt with a cryptographic hash so that no one on the team can edit it afterward
questions.explanation: Code breaks the build the moment it is wrong, but a reworded prompt fails silently and only for some inputs, so a regression suite with a pass threshold is the gate that catches the change before users do.

questions.question: Why does monitoring an LLM pipeline need to look at meaning, not just status codes and latency?
options: Because a model can return a fast 200 response that is confidently wrong, which no uptime or status dashboard catches
Because status codes and latency are in fact the only reliable signals, and every other number is noise in disguise to be ignored
Because token cost cannot be measured without first evaluating every response for meaning and relevance
Because the model changes its weights between calls, so the same prompt has no stable behavior at all
questions.explanation: An LLM can answer quickly with a success status and still be wrong, unsafe, or off topic, so observability has to evaluate responses for quality and drift rather than trust infrastructure metrics alone.

questions.question: What is the core difference between fine-tuning and retrieval augmented generation?
options: RAG changes what the model sees at answer time, while fine-tuning changes how it behaves by altering its weights
RAG retrains the model's weights, while fine-tuning supplies fresh context inside the prompt at run time
Both approaches change the model's weights during training, and they differ only in how much labeled data each one is given
Both leave the model untouched, and they differ only in where the retrieved documents happen to be stored
questions.explanation: Retrieval leaves the weights untouched and feeds the right context at answer time, while fine-tuning continues training so a durable behavior lives inside the model with no retrieval stage in the call path.

questions.question: An agent answers smoothly but keeps formatting its output in prose when a strict structure is required. What kind of gap is this, and which approach fits?
options: A knowledge gap, because the model lacks the specific documents that describe the required output structure
A behavior gap, because the model knows the material but gets the form wrong, which fine-tuning fits
A retrieval gap, because a larger and better-indexed vector store would impose the correct format on the output
A cost gap, because only a smaller and cheaper model can be made to follow the required output structure
questions.explanation: The model knows the content but produces the wrong form, which is a behavior gap: format and style are durable behaviors that fine-tuning is suited to carry in the weights.

questions.question: A support agent needs a consistent brand voice and a strict summary format, plus answers grounded in a policy that changes monthly. What does the framework suggest?
options: Fine-tune only, because baking the policy into the weights is the cheapest way to keep the voice consistent
Retrieve only, because a retrieval layer can also teach the model a consistent voice and output format
A hybrid: fine-tune the durable behavior while retrieval supplies the current facts at answer time
Neither, because you cannot combine a tuned model with a retrieval step in one system
questions.explanation: Voice and format are stable behaviors that fine-tuning can hold, while a policy that changes monthly is current knowledge that retrieval should supply, so the mature answer is the hybrid.
